projectOutComesReport:
The Graduate Student Symposium Planning Committee (GSSPC) is made up of Wayne State University Ph.D. graduate students who have been selected to organize all facets of the GSS including but not limited to choosing the theme, selecting speakers, securing sponsorship, and training the next GSSPC (nGSSPC). Our symposium was held virtually, across two days of the much bigger Spring 2021 American Chemical Society National Meeting and Exposition, held April 9-23, 2021. We selected the theme “Pushing the Boundaries: Women Scientists Catalyzing Change,” centered on the high impact work being done by women scientists all over the country in the field of molecular and nanoscale catalysis. The program of events consisted of a series of research seminars in which we also encouraged our speakers to share the experiences that have shaped their careers, a panel discussion focused on the current climate of women in STEM, and a networking event open to all conference attendees. This symposium served as an opportunity to educate the scientific community on the challenges that continue to affect the representation of women in advance scientific careers, to celebrate the high-impact scientific innovations that women contribute to the field of catalysis in the molecular to nanoscale regime, and to engage early career investigators in the network of the distinguished speakers that we invite. This project led to the conference attendance support of 18 students, 12 of which were first-time national conference attendees, 11 of which gave oral or poster presentations, and over 60% of the selected students were from historically underrepresented backgrounds. Each of our research seminars had 30-40 attendees, and our panel discussion and networking event had 20 participants in each session. These positive experiences, initiated by the events of our symposium have the potential to translate into an increase in the recruitment of early career investigators into the field of catalysis, a rise in the persistence of young women towards degree completion, and an improvement in the sense of community for women and minorities pursuing advanced careers in STEM.

abstractText:
Nontechnical Description:  
Atomically thin semiconductors, referred to as two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, have recently emerged as potential candidate materials for next-generation low-power and high-performance electronics. 2D semiconductors’ atomic flatness, surface-smoothness and thickness-uniformity allow electronic devices, including transistors, to be made smaller and more densely-packed than is currently possible with silicon technology.  Furthermore, the excellent mechanical strength and stretchability of 2D materials also open up new opportunities for next-generation flexible electronics. A critical component of transistors is the metal-semiconductor electrical contacts because charge carriers are injected and extracted through these contacts. In spite of the superb electronic and mechanical properties of 2D semiconductors, the performance of current prototype 2D-semiconductor-based electronic devices is still severely limited by the non-ideal metal-semiconductor contacts. Isolating and understanding which factors limit electrical contacts between metal-electrodes and 2D semiconductors remains a major materials challenge and prevents practical electronic application of 2D semiconductors. To address this knowledge gap, this research uses new methods to controllably modify and characterize the properties of 2D semiconductor interfaces with metals. This project tightly integrates research, education, and community outreach efforts through a series of activities such as summer research for high school students, coaching Science Olympiad teams and lab tours. The emphasis of the education component of this project is placed on promoting diversity through actively recruiting graduate and undergraduate students from underrepresented minority groups. 

Technical Description:
Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors with a suitable bandgap, a reasonably high mobility, excellent mechanical strength and high flexibility are promising channel materials for next generation flexible electronics beyond the scaling limit of silicon-based field-effect transistors. However, a major bottleneck in electronic applications of 2D semiconductors such as transition metal dichalcogenides is their tendency to form a substantial Schottky barrier with most metals at their contacts largely due to Fermi-level pinning effects. This is a strong disadvantage because low-resistance ohmic contacts are needed for realistic devices. The goal of this project is to establish a fundamental understanding of the Fermi-level pinning mechanism at metal/2D-semiconductor interfaces and subsequently develop comprehensive contact-engineering strategies to eliminate the Schottky barrier. This project uses 2D van der Waals contacts with negligible Fermi-level pinning as the baseline and controllably introduce various possible pinning factors to quantitatively understand their roles in Fermi-level pinning.  A variety of materials characterization techniques such as photoelectron spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy will be performed in conjunction with electrical transport measurements to correlate the materials properties with the Schottky barrier height. The knowledge gained from this study is expected to help design effective contact-engineering strategies to achieve ultralow-resistance ohmic contacts to 2D semiconductors, and open up new avenues for basic research on 2D electronic and optoelectronic materials.

abstractText:
The accurate and precise determination of temperature is critical in diagnostic and therapeutic biosystems. Nanomaterials capable of serving as optical temperature sensors are uniquely suited for this task because they are able to operate in environments where contact thermometry cannot be implemented (e.g., cells and deep tissues). However, the vast majority of luminescent nanothermometers lack the required temperature sensitivity. New inorganic nanomaterials with temperature-dependent luminescence response will be discovered and developed in this research. Through a combination of synthesis and characterization studies the rules governing the temperature sensitivity of these phosphors are established. These rules are then used to design optical thermometers with targeted sensitivity within a given temperature window. In addition, this project provides opportunities for workforce development at both undergraduate and graduate levels and K-12 STEM outreach. Graduate and undergraduate students are trained in the synthesis and advanced characterization of luminescent nanomaterials. 6th through 9th grade students participating in the annual STEM Day hosted by Wayne State University are introduced to optical materials research through a hands-on activity based on photostimulable phosphors.

The research aims to develop an understanding of how to tune the temperature sensitivity of luminescent nanothermometers by rationally matching hosts and activators. The chemical and structural tunability of a novel family of host materials is exploited to this end. The project can be divided into three thrust areas. The first area involves synthesis of a series of inorganic nanocrystals that incorporate divalent and trivalent metal dopants as luminescent centers. To this end, colloidal synthetic routes to heterocationic and heteroanionic nanocrystals are developed. The second thrust focuses on ascertaining the placement of the luminescent centers in the nanocrystalline hosts. This task involves interrogating the atomic arrangement in multiple length scales using element-specific spectroscopic probes. Finally, in the third thrust, the temperature-dependent luminescence response of the nanocrystals is systematically probed using steady-state and time-dependent spectrofluorometry. Composition–structure–luminescence relationships are then derived to reveal the fundamental chemical and structural principles governing the temperature sensitivity of the nanothermometers.

projectOutComesReport:
The accurate and precise determination of temperature is critical in medical applications of biophotonics such as cellular-level disease diagnosis and laser ablation therapies. Owing to their ability to function in environments where contact thermometry cannot be implemented and to deliver temperature readings with submicron and subsecond spatiotemporal resolution, nanomaterials capable of serving as luminescent thermometers are uniquely suited for temperature biosensing. Biophotonic applications, however, require luminescent thermometers whose sensitivities can be tailored to peak in a given temperature window. Unfortunately, chemical and structural principles to approach their design from a holistic perspective are lacking. This knowledge gap is a key factor holding back advances in temperature sensors for biophotonic applications. With the support of NSF, our research group has developed an understanding of where to place emitting centers to achieve the desired temperature-dependent luminescence response.

 

Significant results include:

(1) new chemistries to access rare-earth-doped mixed-halide nanocrystals with controlled composition and morphology. Central to this chemistry is the use of heterohaloacetic acids to create metal–organic precursors whose solution thermolysis affords control over nanocrystal nucleation and growth.

(2) the demonstration that the nanocrystals’ temperature-sensing ability may be tuned across the family of alkaline-earth fluorohalides using two levers: (i) the chemical composition of the host, and (ii) the position of the rare-earth dopant(s)’s energy levels within the host bandgap. 

(3) a systematic approach to probe the atomic arrangement of luminescent nanocrystals. This approach entails interrogating atomic correlations in short, intermediate, and long distances. Through this approach, we established that the atomic environment of trivalent rare-earth dopants in fluorohalide nanocrystals consists of hard donors (fluoride and oxygen defects), whereas soft donors (heavy halide ions) are not present. This finding is relevant to understand the role of charge-compensating defects on temperature-dependent luminescence.

(4) the discovery that fluorohaloacetate precursors used in nanocrystal synthesis behave as optical pressure sensors on account of van der Waals interactions responsible for their three-dimensional structure. Two new families of pressure sensors for reduced-pressure environments (<100 mTorr) were thus discovered.

 

These results impacted both the disciplines of photonic materials and materials chemistry by

(1) providing synthetic access to a novel family of luminescent nanothermometers,

(2) uncovering the effect of chemical composition and crystal structure on energy-transfer processes, and

(3) establishing relevant structural and photophysical parameters underlying the luminescence response of rare-earth-doped fluorohalide nanocrystals.

 

Eight peer-reviewed articles totally or partially supported by this Award were published, one more article is currently under review, and one is in preparation. Articles were published in Journal of Materials Chemistry C, Inorganic Chemistry, Dalton Transactions, Journal of Luminescence, and CrystEngComm.  Graduate students supported by this Award presented posters at national and regional conferences including the MRS Fall & Spring Meetings, the ACS National & Central Regional Meetings, and the Rare-Earth Research Conference. The principal investigator gave research seminars at more than 10 academic institutions.

 

This Award provided opportunities for training and professional development of six chemistry graduate students (Ms. Dulani Dhanapala, Mr. Dinesh Amarasinghe, Ms. Hashini Munasinghe, Ms. Nishani Manamperi, Ms. Sachini Sivirathne, and Ms. Dilini Wijepala) and two undergraduate students (Ms. Alyssa Erlenbeck and Ms. Isidora Sekaric). Graduate students were trained in inert atmosphere Schlenk line synthesis and manipulations, solution-based nanocrystal synthesis, powder X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, quantitative crystal structure analysis, and steady-state, time-resolved, and variable-temperature photoluminescence. Ms. Dhanapala, Mr. Amarasinghe, and Ms. Munasinghe also had the opportunity to perform on-site experiments at the Advanced Photon Source of Argonne National Laboratory. Ms. Wijepala was recently selected to participate in the 2025 Neutron and X-ray National School to be held jointly at Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories in July 2025. Dr. Dulani Dhanapala graduated in 2021 and is now a Research Scientist at CEAT (Oklahoma State University). Dr. Dinesh Amarasinghe graduated in October 2020 and is now a Research Scientist at Solid Power Inc. (Louisville, Colorado). Dr. Hashini Munasinghe graduated in 2022 and is now a Scientist at Asbury Carbons (Asbury, New Jersey). Undergraduates B.Sc. Alyssa Erlenbeck and Isidora Sekaric graduated in 2023 and 2024, respectively. The former is now a chemistry Ph.D. candidate at University of Michigan and the latter is a chemistry M.Sc. candidate at University of Windsor (Windsor, Canada). Ms. Erlenbeck coauthored a peer-reviewed article.

 

Educational and outreach activities developed in the context of this Award included:

(1) creation of a module for STEM Day. STEM Day is part of STEM.org, an accredited outreach program, and has been hosted by Wayne State since 2016. During STEM Day, 6th through 9th grade students participate in two hands-on, 40-minute interactive sessions covering the use of storage phosphors. 

(2) annual laboratory tours for 40 students belonging to Western International High School and Cesar Chavez Academy.

(3) writing and English-to-Spanish translation of hands-on activities for a K-12 department outreach activity from 6th, 7th, and 8th grades from Neinas Dual Language Learning Academy, a Detroit Public School.

abstractText:
COVID-19 has disrupted daily work and home lives. More than 297 million people in the U.S. have been placed on full or partial social distancing restrictions. Millions were told to work remotely; others were deemed essential and found themselves on the frontline of this unprecedented pandemic. More than half the schools are closed, leaving more than 33 million children at home. Consequently, millions of dual-income families have been forced to find new ways to balance the competing needs of work and family while maintaining individual and relational well-being. Prior to COVID-19, research consistently showed workers to experience higher work-to-family than family-to-work conflict; however, workers may now experience as high, if not higher, family-to-work conflict given that they have to juggle work and family from the same location: home. Both of these conflicts can have negative effects on individuals and families, including psychological distress, anxiety, anger, guilt, and decreased couple relationship quality. Most studies to date have tested spillover effects of work to family conflict using individual-level data; few have examined the crossover effect with both members included in the analysis, and even fewer longitudinally. This project will survey and interview both adults of dual-income couples at three time points to assess how work, family, and health among dual-income couples have changed within the context of COVID-19.  Findings from this project will inform workplaces on the development of policies to support workers and their families during times of crisis and return-to-work transitions, thus facilitating recovery from this pandemic and preparedness for future extreme events. These are key insights needed to train employers/workers on best practices for employment interventions on family-friendly policies, facilitating organizational change and contributing to healthy workplaces, thus facilitating health and well-being and U. S. economic competitiveness.


Covid-19 has disrupted work and family arrangements owing to school closures, requirements for telework, and social distancing mandates. This project uses a mixed-methods approach by combining surveys and in-depth interviews with both members of a sample of dual-income couples over one year. The project will collect data at three time points: baseline (while most of country is under lockdown orders), transition (after orders start to phase out), and adaptation (one year after the first case of community transmission was detected). The project will use both a traditional single person data analysis strategy, including growth curve modeling and panel regression, and a dyadic data analytical method, the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model, to analyze survey data (n=300 couples; 600 individuals). For the qualitative data, the project will use a thematic analysis to identify emergent patterns on perceptual/behavioral work-family conflict, workplace resources/support, mental health, and relationships. The project will use the qualitative software package NVIVO to manage interview data. Findings from the project will inform sociological theories regarding work-family conflict and accommodation, as well as theories related to the gendered division of household labor.

projectOutComesReport:
COVID-19 has created unprecedented disruptions to home and work lives. This study uses a mixed-methods approach to assess work, family, and social well-being among heterosexual, dual-earning couples in the U.S. over time, within the context of COVID-19. Our sample includes couples with at least one child 17 years or younger living at home (73%) and childfree couples (27%). We collected three waves of survey data with both members of the couple: baseline (n=430 couples; most were under lockdown orders), transition (n=165 couples; after orders began to lift), and adaptation (n=116 couples; 18 months after lockdowns began). We interviewed a subset of couples (n=38) after baseline and adaptation surveys. The dyadic study design allows us to evaluate work, family, and social well-being of the individual and how experiences of one partner cross over to the other partner. Couple-level data are important because partners do not always have sufficient information about the other's lived experiences (e.g., work-family conflict), which leads to "assumed similarity bias," where one may assume another's lived experience is similar to one's own experience. We use individual (e.g., growth curve modeling; panel regression) and dyadic data analytical methods (i.e., the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model; Cook & Kenny 2005; Kenny et al. 2006) to analyze survey data. For the qualitative data, we use a thematic analysis to identify patterns on core outcomes: work-family conflict, workplace resources/support, mental health, and relationships.

The study offers insights into work, family, and social well-being. First, given distinct work configurations during COVID-19, we use a novel scale to measure how the extent of remote work impacts behavioral work-family conflict outcomes (Clark et al. 2019) for each member of a couple and how this crosses over to affect their partner's work-family conflict. We find couples experience higher family-to-work conflict than work-to-family conflict, opposite of most prior research. However, experiences are distinct. Mother's family-to-work conflict and work-to-family conflict increases the more they work remotely but also the more their partner works remotely. In contrast, for non-parents, work-to-family conflict decreases for women and men the more they work remotely. However, the positive impact of one's own remote work on work-to family and family-to work conflict is tempered if their partner also works at home, particularly stronger for women. Our qualitative data supports survey findings; while all parents experience higher family-to-work conflict, the complexity of mothers' narratives reveal work-family struggles, particularly those with flexible schedules; fathers report fewer impacts to their work/home lives.

Second, despite some expectation the gap between women's and men's contribution to housework/caregiving tasks might narrow, our data shows this is not the case. Women assume at least 60% of household physical and mental labor, and significantly so if they both had worked outside the home during the pandemic. Furthermore, 50% or more of couples disagree on who performs about half the physical housework items and almost all the mental labor. For caregiving, couples agree on slightly more items. When couples do not agree, the male partner says they do more of the share of housework/mental labor than credited by their female partner. By including both members of a couple to assess agreement between couples on "who does what," we disentangle biases in self-ratings. Interviews with couples show that women experience a higher burden of housework/caregiving tasks independent of work location; their male partner largely agrees.

Third, results highlight social well-being outcomes. Analyses suggest the mental health of parents of minor children, measured by psychological distress, is impacted more negatively by the onset of COVID-19 and daily life restrictions. Additionally, the pandemic influences how couples employ individual, social, and communal coping strategies to manage distress. Interview data finds couples use three metaphors to explain coping: conflict highlighting incompatibility, fiction highlighting sur-reality/uncertainty, and control highlighting feelings of little influence over their situation.

Findings offer broader impacts. Findings may inform workplaces on policy development to support workers and their families as they implement return-to-work transitions (e.g., flextime/place; supervisor/organizational support), facilitating pandemic recovery and preparedness for future extreme events. However, given gendered and parental status findings, a "one-size-fits all" approach is unlikely to be effective. These are key insights to train employers/workers on best practices for employment interventions on family-friendly policies, fostering organizational change, contributing to healthy workplaces, and supporting U.S. economic competitiveness.

Another broader impact is that COVID-19 may have uncovered mental health differences among different groups. The negative impact of the lack of childcare and flexibility, for example, on mental health, evident prior to the pandemic, may have increased during the pandemic. The results of our study call on policy makers and employers to provide working adults the formal (e.g., affordable/reliable family caregiving supports) and informal work-life supports (e.g., discouraging 24/7 connectivity to work through electronic communications) necessary to improve mental health outcomes of both employees and their family.

abstractText:
This project will develop a web-based tool that allows for easy visualization of seismic wave propagation through the earth. By offering instant access to analysis, visualization, and rock-based data, this tool will foster cross-disciplinary research and lower the threshold for scientists from several communities to engage with seismic wave studies, particularly for students and early career scientists. The web tool will also provide easy classroom use. The project will organize two workshops on seismic anisotropy using the tool, focusing on support for student and early career investigators, as well as development of a teaching module that will be made available through the Carleton College Science Education Resource Center (SERC) repository. The project will fund an undergraduate research assistant and a female scientific team. 

Seismic anisotropy is of increasing interest to researchers from several Earth science communities because it offers a rare avenue to imaging present-day and past deformation processes at depth. Deformation in the deep crust and mantle leads to the development of mineral fabric which produces seismic anisotropy. This team of researchers hold a database of crustal rock-based elasticity tensors. This project will develop a web-based tool that ties to the database and offers the following capabilities: 1. Interactive calculation and visualization with rotation of seismic parameters for tensors in the database within a deformation reference frame, as well as of any elasticity tensor pasted in by the user; 2. Tensor decomposition into symmetry components and visualization of results, allowing the user to answer questions such as how well the tensor is represented by a simplified symmetry such as hexagonal or orthorhombic, and in the former case by a fast or slow symmetry axis; 3. Averaging of bulk elasticity over several rock compositions or folded geometries. Given that there are several ongoing efforts funded by programs such as EarthCube to bring field structural geology and microstructural analysis into the big data domain (e.g., MacroStrat, Strabo), including results such as electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) maps of samples, a future effort could tie the web tool to be developed to such projects in order to provide elasticity tensor analysis based on data held in these applications.

abstractText:
Since 2010, there has been a rapid increase in children who seek medical and psychological services related to the stress they experience regarding the nonconformity between their assigned sex at birth (male or female) and how they experience their gender in daily life (male, female, both, or neither), also known as gender dysphoria. There has been significant concern about the mental health of these youth, especially concerning the risk of adverse mental health events, including suicide. However, research shows that when nonconforming adolescents are well-supported, they have similar levels of depression to other adolescents. For such adolescents who seek medical intervention, these support systems may include parents as advocates and/or healthcare professionals who specialize in serving them. In these cases, decisions about steps towards intervention are made between the adolescents, their parents, as well as the physicians. Findings from this in-depth interview study will help inform healthcare professionals about ways in which medical services can improve for these adolescents. This research will also provide information for families and other stakeholders about how to advance the health and wellbeing of adolescents.  This project provides a platform for adolescents to describe their lived experiences, which can benefit the medical field and families that need their expertise.

Studying gender non-conforming adolescents provides researchers with the opportunity to analyze the processes that contribute to the creation of their identities.  This project will explain how non-conforming adolescents who receive medical interventions address the complexity of their identities. Data collection involves 60 in-depth, semi-structured face-to-face interviews with three groups: 20 non-conforming adolescents, 20 parents of such adolescents, and 20 physicians who work with such adolescents.  Participants in this study will be identified through a combination of personal contacts and snowball sampling. Interview questions with physicians include exploring reasons for approving or denying medical services to adolescents, how they help facilitate discussions between parents and adolescents, and ways in which healthcare for these adolescents can be improved. Interviews with the parents focus on their child’s behaviors and interactions with doctors. Questions with the adolescents will probe for reasons behind their decisions to seek information about medical intervention and their experiences with this process. Interview data will be subjected to open coding to derive themes present in the data using NVIVO to manage transcripts and data analysis. This project addresses the gap in our knowledge on the behaviors and beliefs of non-conforming adolescents and will provide insight into medical technologies to support them. Findings will also inform sociological theories related to gender and social identities, particularly for adolescents as they transition to adulthood.

Research shows that when gender non-conforming young people are well-supported throughout their gender transition they have similar levels of depression to their cisgender counterparts. For gender non-conforming young people who wish to transition medically, these support systems may include parents as advocates or healthcare professionals who specialize in gender non-conforming services. Decisions about steps throughout transition are made between gender non-conforming children, their parents, as well as the physicians. This dissertation aims to shed light on the shared-decision making process between gender non-conforming adolescents, parents, and healthcare providers throughout medical transition. Through interviews with these three groups, this study provides critical insights into the decision making process and how medicalization impacts the identity construction of transgender adolescents. Its findings can help healthcare professionals and parents learn better ways to approach transition that works to respect an adolescent patient’s autonomy, while holding critical dialogue that simultaneously affirms their identity.

Overall, this study uncovers the various ways adolescents are medicalized throughout the gender transition process and how parents and healthcare professionals impact their identity construction. I draw on evidence from this dissertation to expand on gender structure theory (Risman, 2004; 2018; Scarborough & Risman, 2017) as an analytical framework and to provide insights into the ways that cultural gendered ideologies effect transgender adolescent healthcare. Although every person is regulated by gender norms and expectations, my data reveals the scrutinized process that transgender adolescents go through because they must gain approval from very influential social structures (families, mental health professionals, and physicians) before they are able to receive services that support their overall well-being. abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is to develop technology to make the low-altitude airspace more accessible for commercial drone delivery operations while ensuring a high level of operational safety and efficiency. Large-scale, organized deployment of delivery drones can unlock substantial efficiency gain in transportation systems in terms of reduced road congestion, reduced CO2 emission; in addition, it would offer health and convenience benefits to senior citizens, the ill, and mobility-challenged members of society. However, existing drone delivery practices are limited in scope, scale, and operating conditions due to inefficient air traffic management (ATM) paradigms. This project aims to discover a viable business model for translating technological innovations in unmanned ATM into an operable, city-scale, fully automated drone delivery system. The proposed system would allow safe use of the low-altitude airspace at an unprecedented density and efficiency, generating enormous savings for last-mile deliveries. 

This I-Corps project explores the development of a suite of novel optimization-driven algorithms in the areas of motion-planning, dynamic vehicle routing, communication and risk minimization to provide real-time ATM and trajectory control for a cooperative fleet of drones navigating a shared airspace. Existing ATM methods leave excessive separation margins due to human-level response time and control dexterity. In contrast, the proposed new system is optimized for high-density air traffic conditions, offering the capability to generate real-time adjustments to 4D flight trajectories, tolerating a smaller separation margin, and overseeing safe execution of control commands across the fleet. In a plug-and-play fashion, the proposed system will turn a collection of heterogeneous multicopter drones into an organized and intelligent fleet. The competitive advantage lies in the fusion of the state-of-the-art operations research (OR) models and algorithms onto drone platforms via commoditized cloud computing, IoT and communication infrastructures.

projectOutComesReport:
The primary goal of the project was to discover a pathway for translating optimization-driven high-density air traffic management (UTM) algorithms into a viable business model. A critical first step is understanding who will benefit from this technology, who will pay for it and how much they are willing to pay. A secondary goal was to gather practical insights, including previously overlooked pain points of drone users and new use cases, to direct future R&D and commercialization endeavors.

Through customer interviews, site visits, community engagement and tradeshows, the team has gathered tremendous first-hand information about the UTM ecosystem, and tested many hypotheses about technology readiness, value proposition, and customer segments. The team interviewed more than 100 people that were hypothesized to play key roles in the drone delivery ecosystem, if one was established. Here are some key findings. 1. For small drones, while the cost of electric energy consumed in a short flight is almost negligible, the flight’s share of the battery’s acquisition and maintenance costs is not. Barring a new breakthrough in battery technology (or alternative power source technology), efficient fleet-level battery management will be the key factor that determines the bottom line of a drone-based delivery business. 2. The DJI drones and software suites have been predominantly used in production and revenue-generating missions of small multirotor aircraft, in spite of federal and state level rulemaking movements against foreign-made drones. 3. The need for optimization (of drone traffic) in the context of USS interoperability is lukewarm. One reason is the lack of a standard cost model for the use of low-altitude airspace.

This I-Corps project provided the entrepreneurial lead (EL) in-depth knowledge of the lean startup process. The EL used the learning to build and grow a team and launched Litter-Robot 4, a new generation of self-cleaning litter box for pets. This project has led the EL to pursue an entrepreneurial career where he worked with several startups in various roles. Customer discovery activities and findings enabled the technical lead (TL) to better align his R&D efforts with market needs. The TL learned to ask the right questions and focus on customer discovery before any product development. The Co-TL obtained his PhD degree with support of this project and landed his first job as R&D scientist in an insurance firm. The industrial mentor launched his own startup company in a different area (K-12 student transportation) and continued practicing the I-Corps mindsets and techniques, including doing the job of driving a bus for 6 weeks to understand customer needs and pain points.

The objective of this renewal Summer Academy in Sustainable Manufacturing REU is to expose undergraduate students to the forefront of sustainable manufacturing research at Wayne State University in Detroit, MI, a historical hub of United States manufacturing. The Summer Academy in Sustainable Manufacturing serves a national priority area in advanced manufacturing and sustainability, and offers multi-disciplinary sustainable manufacturing undergraduate research projects. Participants research challenging manufacturing sustainability problems, strengthen communication and networking skills, and are prepared to pursue graduate degrees. Site projects cross-cut materials science, product design, process design, manufacturing systems, and sustainable engineering, and integrate the fundamental approaches of sustainable manufacturing into these areas. The site’s recruitment plan is aimed at attracting a diverse set of students interested in undergraduate research, particularly from underrepresented minority groups, in order to create a vibrant sustainable manufacturing research community. The site’s training model, which provides a dynamic environment for student research and broad communication with a diverse faculty team and industrial practitioners, aims to set an example for other sustainability and sustainable manufacturing communities in the nation. Participants develop self-learning, engineering research, and technical communication skills under the supervision of faculty mentors from the Wayne State Industrial and Systems Engineering, Chemical Engineering and Materials Science, Mechanical Engineering, and Electrical and Computer Engineering Departments, in addition to participating in community building activities that include visits to the Detroit Institute of Arts and Charles H. Wright African American History Museum.

The REU Site research and training activities prepare participants to be the next generation of sustainable manufacturing engineers and researchers, a field that is continuously growing in relevance and necessity to industry and society, yet severely lacking in expertise. Target participants for the Summer Academy are underrepresented minority students who traditionally have little access to undergraduate research opportunities or may not have otherwise considered graduate studies a feasible career pathway. The REU Site fosters long-term contributions to sustainable manufacturing knowledge from continuing mentor/mentee relationships and undergraduate research project outcomes in eco-friendly batteries, sustainable nano-manufacturing, remanufacturing via additive manufacturing, biofuels production systems, and life-cycle cyber-learning, to list a few. During the 10 week summer program, participants of the Summer Academy in Sustainable Manufacturing participate in five research seminars covering critical areas of sustainable manufacturing research, four skill development seminars that prepare participants for research and graduate programs, three site visits to local manufacturing companies (Ford Rouge Factory, BASF polyurethane manufacturing plant, and Lightweight Innovations for Tomorrow, LIFT, institute), and three industry guest lectures that focus on sustainability in large scale manufacturing. Concurrently, participants work in faculty mentor laboratories on next generation sustainable manufacturing research challenges to advance the knowledge of sustainability in manufacturing and experience academic research first-hand.

projectOutComesReport:
The REU Site: Summer Academy in Sustainable Manufacturing project continued an existing ten week undergraduate summer research program at Wayne State University for domestic undergraduate students to experience cutting edge research laboratories, investigate sustainable manufacturing technology challenges, and develop skills essential to pursuing careers in sustainable manufacturing research and industry practice. Sustainable manufacturing is defined as the creation of manufactured products that use processes that minimize negative environmental impacts; conserve energy and natural resources; are safe for employees, communities, and consumers; and are economically sound. Transferring sustainable manufacturing principles into the next-generation manufacturing of researchers and practitioners contributes to enhancing US manufacturing global competitiveness and strategic vision. This REU Site’s metropolitan location in midtown Detroit, MI and its vicinity to the US automotive manufacturing offered participants a unique experience, enabling participants to experience the resurgence of Detroit, MI, interact with historically significant manufacturing companies, and research sustainability issues facing manufacturing.

The REU Site received significant interest from undergraduate students across the US who were from more than twenty engineering and non-engineering disciplines. In total, the site received two hundred forty-six applications from one hundred twenty-three universities and institutions of higher education from across the nation. Approximately half of all applications were from underrepresented minorities in science and engineering or those with little to no access to undergraduate research opportunities in sustainable manufacturing. Thirty-three undergraduate students participated and completed the site program. Site participants came from a variety of regions in the US, including the west coast, east coast, midwest, southeast, and central US, and approximately half of the participants were underrepresented minorities in science and engineering or those with little to no access to undergraduate research opportunities in sustainable manufacturing.  

REU site participants made contributions to multiple, critical sustainable manufacturing research thrusts. A partial list of research project that participants contributed to including but not limited to: characterizing surface geometry and defects using laser line scanning for remanufacturing, energy efficiency in mobile augmented reality apps, modeling the sustainability of electroplating systems, rare earth element adsorption with metal organic frameworks, augmented reality human interactions with robotic manufacturing systems, new design strategies for Lithium-Ion batteries, scalable nano-manufacturing, energy efficiency and carbon dioxide emission analysis of geographically distributed manufacturing, and silver nano-wire ink development for neuromorphic computing. To date, site undergraduate research projects and site activities have contributed to four journal publications, nine conference publications/presentations, and eight undergraduate research poster presentations at national conferences. Site participants presented their research projects at the Council of Undergraduate Research Undergraduate Research Symposium, and the REU Site program, as a whole, was presented at the 2022 American Society for Engineering Education Annual Conference's NSF grantees poster symposium and the 2025 International Congress on Sustainability Science and Engineering (ICOSSE) in Auckland, New Zealand. In addition to laboratory research and site commitments, participants explored surrounding areas and cities such as Toronto, Canada and Chicago, Illinois, and visited local museums such as the Detroit Historical Society, Detroit Institute of Arts, the Ford Rouge Factory Tour at the Henry Ford, and the Ford Piquette Plant Museum. Co-hort activities cultivated the REU site community, which served to enhance weekly group meetings where participants learned the skills necessary to confidently present their research to peers and academia.

Feedback from site evaluation surveys was overwhelmingly positive. Overall, 86% of participants felt satisfied with the entire REU site experience, and 71% of participants indicated that their research mentor was above average, with 43% indicated their research mentor was outstanding. Evaluation results also demonstrated that the program design was effective at improving the participants’ level of knowledge of advanced manufacturing and engineering sustainability. Participant advanced manufacturing knowledge increased from 28% rated as high or somewhat high pre-reu site program to 80% rated as high or somewhat high post-reu site program. Participant engineering sustainability knowledge increased from 53% rated as high or somewhat high pre-reu site program to 93% rated as high or somewhat high post-reu site program. More information about the Summer Academy in Sustainable Manufacturing, participants, and undergraduate research projects can be found on our website (https://advancedmaterials.wayne.edu/summer-academy) or by contacting the PIs.

abstractText:
An unanticipated harmful algal bloom (HAB) appeared in Lake Anna, Virginia in early August, 2019. Lake Anna is one of the largest freshwater reservoirs in VA. Research is needed to understand threats, manage risks, mitigate incidents, develop capabilities, and strengthen collaborations for our water safety and security. Aerial and aquatic robots will work alongside health and water quality experts from VDH and DEQ to (1) help inform their regular sampling efforts, and (2) provide critical and timely information to guide regulatory decisions.  The HAB is still going at Lake Anna, and it is expected to continue until the first freeze at the Lake. Once the first freeze occurs, most of the cyanobacteria will explode and unload a large amount of toxins, requiring further analysis.

Since the first report of the harmful algal boom (HAB) on Lake Anna, the bloom has reportedly intensified, and the Virginia Department of Health (VDH) has issued multiple advisories. The most recent VDH advisory (issued on Sept 20, 2019) showed the HAB extending down both northern branches of the lake. The VDH advisories are based in part on water quality data from the VA Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ), which collects samples from a series of stations (GPS waypoints where a manned boat is used to collect samples by hand) across the lake. The research team will work alongside water quality experts (DEQ and VDH) to make targeted collections of the HAB at Lake Anna using aerial robots (a drone equipped with multispectral sensors to image the bloom and a device to sample the water) and aquatic robots (a remotely operated underwater vehicle equipped with underwater GPS, sensors to track the plume in situ, and a device to collect underwater samples). These samples will be analyzed for toxins and nutrients, and the data will be shared with water quality experts and members of the Lake Anna Civic Association. Based on 10 years of seasonal toxin data for Grand Lake St. Marys in Ohio, the research team hypothesize that (1) the HAB at Lake Anna, VA will continue to progress and produce high toxin levels through the coming winter months and (2) aerial and aquatic robots can identify, localize, and sample targeted areas of the HAB in the lake. The specific objectives of this project are to (1) use aerial and aquatic robots to target the HAB in Lake Anna, VA and collect samples at strategic locations; and (2) determine toxin concentrations and nutrient loads in samples collected by robots working alongside humans. This information is critical for determining time-sensitive health advisories, and for the communities of people that live in and around the lake. This work will also show the value of unmanned systems to assist stakeholders in tracking HABs in the water; resulting field-tested technology will provide decision-makers with co-robots that can provide rapid and detailed information on the dispersal of HABs in the environment.  The HAB is still going at Lake Anna, and it is expected to continue until the first freeze at the Lake. Once the first freeze occurs, most of the cyanobacteria will lyse and unload a copious amount of cyanotoxins.

projectOutComesReport:
Harmful algal blooms are increasing in frequency due to nutrient rich runoff across the Midwest and eastern United States. Nutrient rich non-point runoff serves to catalyze bloom activity which fouls water by degrading aesthetic, palatability, increasing toxicity, and reducing recreation potential. The effects can be related to public health, economic, and biological declines. The objective of this project is to analyze nutrients and algal activity associated with water samples taken from Lake Anna, Virginia, in an effort to better understand bloom activity. This project was conducted as a team effort among leading experts in targeted autonomous sampling drones (PI – David Schmale PhD, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University) as well as algal toxin analysis (Co-PI Judy Westrick PhD, Wayne State University).

  1. Rapid real time collections were made of water samples from Lake Anna in 2020 and were analyzed for phycocyanin, nutrients, toxins, and spatial disparity.
  2. Analyses and observations served as critical pivot points for local advisement regarding the lake condition and carried implications for human health and environmental condition.
  3. Rapid deployment of field technologies in conjunction with lab analyses provide a potential template for managing information in algal blooms elsewhere.
  4. Nutreint analyses were performed on all samples.
  5. Targeted cyanotoxin and cyanopeptide analyses were performed on the the samples. Cyanotoxin were detected at the low part-per-trillion levels.

The outcomes from this project was shared with the Lake Anna community and will be used in developing a HAB predictive model.

abstractText:
With support from the Chemical Measurement and Imaging Program in the Division of Chemistry, Professor Long Luo and his group at Wayne State University are working to develop a powerful new approach for the identification and quantitative analysis of an important class of chemical compounds.  Specifically, they are targeting molecules known as surfactants, which are widely used as emulsifiers, detergents, fabric softeners, and wetting agents in many household cleaners and industrial products and processes. Naturally occurring surfactants such as glycolipids, lipopeptides, lipoproteins, fatty acids, neutral lipids, and phospholipids are also essential to the functioning of biological systems. Current methods for surfactant analysis do not detect specific products (selectivity) and low concentrations (sensitivity). Professor Luo and his group are developing new electrochemical approaches to address these challenges. They are also working on applying the tools for on-site detection of polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a group of emerging surfactants that are contaminants of concern in drinking water. The integrated educational aims of this work seek to increase STEM awareness, interest, and career preparedness across a range of ages, educational levels, and socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds by performing science shows at public locations; developing STEM exposure programs for middle and high school students; and establishing and running a student chapter of the Electrochemical Society at Wayne State University.  Notably, the team will reach out to the public about the relevance of science in everyday life by organizing and performing a science show at the Great Lakes Crossing Outlets Mall and Detroit Zoo, the two largest family attractions in Michigan.

Limited selectivity and sensitivity have been a long-standing problem in surfactant analysis. To address these issues, the Luo group is using the gas bubble-surfactant interaction to establish a selective and sensitive detection method coupled with rapid and efficient preconcentration. Specifically, the unique amphiphilic characteristics of surfactants affect electrochemical gas bubble nucleation, which in turn impacts an electrochemical signal used for the quantification of surfactants. An approach mimicking sea-spray aerosol enrichment is used to preconcentrate the surfactants. These features are being combined in a portable device to address the unmet need for on-site detection of PFAS in drinking water, addressing concerns arising from U.S. Environmental Protection Agency identification of PFAS quantitation as a national priority. Broader impacts of the educational plan include increasing public interest in science and technology, promoting middle and high school students’ engagement in analytical chemistry activities, and boosting undergraduate and graduate students’ interest in electrochemistry.

The project will provide support for graduate student participation in the 17th International Congress on Catalysis (ICC) to be held in San Diego, California (CA) on June 14-19, 2020.  Specifically, the funding will partially cover registration and travel expenses of approximately 35 U.S. academic PhD students to attend the Congress and facilitate their interaction with the international catalysis community. The students will present their research at the conference, attend lectures by leaders in the field of catalysis, and interact with fellow students from around the world. 

The ICC meetings are the largest global meeting dedicated to catalysis, and are held once every four years. The Congress was last held in the United States in 1996.  The theme of 17th ICC - 2020 Vision for Catalysis - aims to look into the future for catalysis research guided by the past and to assess the present state of catalysis in context of what lies ahead. The program will highlight recent developments,challenges, and opportunities in the context of shifting feedstocks and in the discovery and development of experimental and computational methods. The scientific program will include plenary and keynote lectures, invited and ontributed papers and poster presentations. The proceedings of all International Congresses are published as abstracts on the web. They also constitute a significant part of the archival literature on catalysis. The critical importance of catalysis is reflected by the fact that 25-30% of all manufactured goods in the United States involve at least one catalytic step. Because advances in a large number of catalytic processes, which are crucial to U.S. interests, will be presented at this meeting, it is important to ensure participation from both the U.S. academic and the industrial sectors. Furthermore, the International Congress is a rare opportunity for U.S. students to interact with fellow students and premier researchers from all across the world at the most prestigious conference the catalysis community has to offer. This will significantly assist with maintaining U.S. research competitiveness, while also inspiring students to tackle grand challenges related to catalytic processes. Catalysis is an enabling technology for a broad range of scientific and engineering impact areas related to environmental pollution control, sustainability, energy, and chemicals, to name just a few. Student training and engagement in these areas ensures a future crop of catalytic researchers well-positioned to make continued advances to science and engineering that will serve the needs of the Nation and society in general for years to come.

abstractText:
Autonomous Robot (AR) fleets will soon assist humans for the execution of several tasks. One of the most important factors that will likely affect the widespread adoption of AR fleets in our society is their ease of management for the end users. The goal of this project is to achieve the easy management of the AR fleet by allowing end users to indicate the set of tasks to execute during a working period and by implementing algorithms that automatically (i) allocate tasks to ARs, (ii) coordinate recharge schedules, (iii) ensure continuity of operations, and (iv) minimize the battery degradation. 

The intellectual merits of this project are focused on designing an AR fleet manager system that can be used by end users to interact easily with an AR fleet. Three main research thrusts are: (i) joint optimization of concurrent tasks allocation and recharge scheduling for ARs to minimize the task downtime and battery degradation during the working period; (ii) coordination of the ARs' computing and sensing resources to balance tasks performance and energy consumption; (iii) full system implementation and experimentation on a small-scale physical testbed and a large-scale simulated testbed. 

The proposed work will introduce new technologies available for the management of AR fleets and boost the widespread use of autonomous robots in our society, e.g., homes, smart farms, industry, and smart cities. The project will provide a new hardware and software testbed to help train and inspire undergraduate and graduate students. New industry collaborations will be established to enhance AR adoption. New academic collaborations will also be established with researchers in various areas including robotics, artificial intelligence, control systems, sensing, and approximation algorithms. 

All the new algorithms and the experimental results generated as part of the proposed project will be distributed in the form of journal articles, conference proceedings, workshops, invited presentations, and student thesis. In addition, the data, source code, simulators, and hardware details will be maintained on a dedicated research website (http://brok.eng.wayne.edu/AFM.html). This repository will be retained and maintained for at least five years after the completion of the project.

projectOutComesReport:
We have developed an Autonomous robots Fleet Manager, which jointly considers the problem of minimizing the downtime of computational task execution and the battery lifespan degradation for a fleet of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs). This is the first study conducted to address the problem of how to trade off task performance and battery lifespan for battery-powered computing systems. Our specific objectives were to develop an Integrated Task Allocation and Charging Manager (TCM), and a per-robot power manager. TCM runs on a local server node. It periodically updates the task allocation on the AMRs and their recharge schedule to ensure continuity of operations for the remaining working period while preserving the batteries' lifetime. On each AMR, the power manager runs at a finer time grain than TCM to modulate the computing speed and the robot speed so that the tasks performance is maximized under a power cap indicated by the TCM. In addition, the project helped building a small-scale fleet of AMRs in the Energy-aware autonomous systems lab of the PI and to explore collaborations on battery lifespan-aware sensor networks, collaborative battery-based vehicle computing, and real-time systems.

We have designed TCM, a polynomial time algorithm that allocates tasks and schedules charges to minimize downtime while maximizing the battery life quality of an AMR fleet. Its decisions are affected by a weight parameter that allows users to choose the importance on the battery life quality target over task allocation performance. 

We have studied how to handle fault tolerance by scheduling preventive robot maintenance and by leveraging task replication for task allocation. For the first approach, we handle the high problem complexity by designing an algorithm based on linear programming and a variant of Hungarian method to schedule robot maintenance and to optimally allocate tasks/charging for each robot. For the second approach, we have designed a framework for energy-aware resource management in collaborative autonomous vehicle computing systems. The framework is composed of two algorithms: (i) a resource selector algorithm that determines which vehicles can share their resources for task allocation and improved fault tolerance over an optimized sharing period; and (ii) an energy manager algorithm that determines the task allocation across vehicles and how many replicas to use for each task with the aim of minimizing the computational energy consumption while satisfying a desired risk factor.

We have worked on how to provide real-time guarantees considering a system of primary-secondary processor, where the primary processor is mainly used but can offload tasks to the secondary processor when deadlines would be missed. This is applicable to many autonomous systems, including robots, where multiple computing units are available either on board or remotely. 

To further investigate the opportunity of using edge servers assisting the navigation software of autonomous robots/vehicles, we have also worked on studying how heterogeneous edge computing systems affect their navigation speed. Specifically, we have studied how robot/vehicle safe speed and travel time on a selected path is affected by deploying different amounts of resources in different areas where autonomous vehicles/robots operate. The insights and findings of this study will inspire new research that can considerably speed up the deployment of edge-assisted autonomous mobile systems in our society.

We have built and programmed three autonomous mobile robots, which are now able to autonomously navigate an indoor environment with fixed and moving obstacles. Using this fleet, we have collected data on energy consumption and timeliness of navigation task execution to determine how to best use the energy budget provided by TCM while maximizing task performance and safety. In particular, we have used the collected data to design a lightweight imitation learning-based control system that dynamically decides computing frequency and robot speed directly on the robot for optimized performance. 

In relation to battery lifespan-aware computing, we have worked on a network protocol able to trade off performance of packet transmission for longer battery lifespan in energy-harvested sensor nodes. The work was tested in both simulation and real environment.

We have involved two PhD students as well as four undergraduate students in this project, including two female underrepresented students. We have published the above research in IEEE International Conference on Autonomic Computing and Self-Organizing Systems (ACSOS), IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing, IEEE International Conference on Embedded Software and Systems (ICESS), and some, at the time of writing, are being reviewed by IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems and other reputable conferences. We will leverage the small-scale autonomous mobile robot fleet and the gained experience to conduct further research on environmental sustainability of battery-based autonomous systems. We have created a website for the project and made our TCM implementation open source and downloadable from github.
